page: Google Cloud Platform g4-standard-384 is an accelerator-focused instance type positioned within the GPU Machines family. The platform couples high-density host compute capacity with dedicated graphics hardware to serve demanding multi-GPU enterprise workloads. Built on the x86_64 instruction set architecture, the system provides 384 dedicated virtual central processing units alongside 1440 GB of system memory, establishing a host resource density of 3.75 GB of RAM per vCPU.

Hardware acceleration is driven by eight NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs from the Blackwell generation, which contribute a combined total of 768 GB of video RAM. This large graphics memory pool allows simultaneous handling of extensive visual scenes, rendering pipelines, or parallel compute tasks across all eight physical accelerators. The instance does not include integrated local disk storage or complimentary public IPv4 networking addresses, making persistent network disks and private networking configurations standard prerequisites for deployment.

In terms of qualitative efficiency, consolidating eight discrete professional GPUs and 384 host cores into a single virtual machine minimizes communication latency across accelerators compared to distributed multi-node clusters. The primary trade-off centers on storage and networking: with no integrated local NVMe storage, total data throughput relies strictly on attached cloud volumes and network fabrics. The hardware profile is aligned with graphics-optimized tasks, 3D simulation, offline rendering pipelines, and large-scale visual compute applications that require high aggregate VRAM and dense host thread counts.

Acceleration is delivered via eight NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs based on the Blackwell architecture, yielding 768 GB of aggregate video memory. The configuration contains no local storage, requiring persistent or networked storage solutions for workload deployment, and includes zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses. The heavy concentration of parallel execution units alongside substantial host and GPU memory addresses large-scale visual processing and high-throughput rendering workloads. From a qualitative resource profile perspective, aggregating eight high-tier GPUs into a single host eliminates inter-node communication overhead for multi-GPU graphics jobs, though users must manage storage I/O remotely.
